title: Upbringing: LLM Post-Training
summary: Experiments in teaching language models through examples, preferences, and rewards.
contribution: I developed the experiments, evaluation, and interactive study with AI assistance, using existing models and training methods.
details: Three small-scale studies: instruction tuning on OLMo 2, preference learning with simulated labelers, and reinforcement learning on Countdown arithmetic with Qwen2.5-3B.

Countdown accuracy rose from 1.3% to 55.7% per attempt on 256 development-monitored puzzles. An earlier run also exposed an answer-extraction bug in the grader; it did not establish learned reward hacking.
usage: Explore the interactive study to compare model responses, or use the repository and published checkpoints to inspect the experiments.

title: Cognanimus
summary: An adaptive learning platform with lessons, practice, feedback, and progress tracking.
contribution: I designed and built the learning flows, grading, and progress tracking with AI assistance.
details: Choose a learning path and work through lessons and assessments. Structured answers use programmatic checks; written answers receive model-generated feedback. Saved attempts and follow-up questions help track what you retain.
usage: The website is an invite-only alpha. Learning effectiveness has not yet been evaluated in a learner study.

title: Busy Beaver Challenge
summary: AI-assisted work on the Busy Beaver Challenge: proving whether small Turing machines halt or run forever.
contribution: I directed the search and submitted contributions. Claude Code produced the merged proofs and Rocq formalizations, checked with BusyCoq.

primaryLink.label: Open research dashboard
primaryLink.note: Static snapshot of the research dashboard.

details: The dashboard collects machine simulations, proof writeups, and contributions to BusyCoq. It shows how a tiny program can produce behavior that is difficult to understand, even after billions of simulated steps.
usage: Open the dashboard, pick a machine, and explore its tape diagram, proof, or interactive simulator. The dashboard is a dated static copy.

title: AI Safety Research
eyebrow: What keeps an AI agent from taking a harmful shortcut?
summary: Experiments on refusal, harmful shortcuts, and how behavior transfers between language-model agents.
contribution: I set the research direction, with AI-assisted implementation and analysis. Claude ran the latest experimental sprint autonomously.
details: What happens when a model’s internal refusal direction is removed? These studies compare an edited Qwen3.8-27B with the original and control edits in simulated tasks offering a safe route, a harmful shortcut, and a hand-off to a human.

The latest study found that removing refusal increased compliance with direct harmful orders, but usually left restraint intact in agentic tasks. The main shortcut effect was small and statistically fragile. A later, exploratory low-effort run and changes to how harm was described produced larger effects.

Follow-ups examine student distillation, multi-agent oversight, reviewer advice, and activation probes. Students learned some shortcut-taking from the edited model’s transcripts; the mechanism remains unresolved. Several multi-agent tests hit floors or ceilings and could not establish safety.

The project began with curiosity and satisfaction experiments, which found limited or absent steering effects. The current safety work includes strict tool-call scoring, analysis records, and checks connecting reported numbers to those records.
usage: Start with the plain-language summary in the latest study, then explore the code, experimental plan, and analysis records in the repository.
note: The scenarios were calibrated on the original model, and most results use one greedy response per item. The October 18–19, 2026 v3 study supersedes earlier safety results. Raw transcripts are not included in the public repository.
